newsitem.title: USA: Some retailers to be mum about sales this Christmas.
newsitem.headline: Some retailers to be mum about sales this Christmas.

text.p: A growing number of store chains will be mum about holiday sales this season just as skittsh investors crave more information about the volatile retailing industry.

Retailers such as Abercrombie & Fitch Co., Loehmann's Inc. and Gucci Group N.V. see many drawbacks revealing whether their cash registers are full around Christmas. Unlike most store chains, which disclose sales at least once a month, they will report sales quarterly, or semiannually in Gucci's case.

By reporting sales less frequently, they believe they give a better picture of business strategies. They also seek to avoid swings in the price of their stock, which often becomes volatile as a result of the monthly reports.
But in these rocky times for retailers, the lack of information makes some experts anxious. After a tidal wave of bankruptcies last year, they are hungry for more data, not less.

"Shareholders have been badly treated by the industry and should be wary," said Nell Minow, principal with the shareholder activist group LENS. "But I'm also sympathetic to retailers for not wanting people to make snap judgments."

In many ways, Wall Street analysts support stores that report sales quarterly. It makes retailing executives less tempted to resort to quick fixes -- like last-minute merchandise markdowns -- to pump up sales in weak months.

On the other hand, retailers like Nordstrom Inc. that disclose volume just once a quarter leave observers hanging for so long that they are often disappointed when the news finally arrives, analysts noted.
If last year's ho-hum holiday shopping season is any guide, retailers have good reason to keep a low profile.

A blizzard in the Northeast the week before Christmas 1995 along with soft consumer spending socked retail stocks hard. And this year's compressed shopping season with five fewer days between Thanksgiving and Christmas also promises to be a challenge for the industry.

During the weeks leading up to Dec. 25, many stores will discuss customer traffic every week. When last year's storm hit, for example, J.C. Penney Co. Inc., Federated Department Stores Inc. and Sears, Roebuck and Co. all acknowledged the next day that business had slowed.

Hurricanes and hot TV programmes like the Olympics also keep shoppers away, briefly stifling sales. But most of these events are short-lived and usually don't influence a full quarter's profits. Explaining these blips to outsiders sometimes is just a waste of time, retailers said.

When Indian summer weather put a drag on apparel sales last month, Dayton Hudson Corp., parent of the discount chain Target and Marshall Field's department stores, told Wall Street that sales had turned weak.
This sent the company's shares down to $30.75, or about 14 percent below their recent high. Two weeks later, the stock had recovered about half of the lost value.
Menomonee Falls, Wis.-based Kohl's Corp. used to talk to Wall Street every week but stopped a couple years ago.

"There are just too many factors on a week-to-week basis" that buffet consumer demand, said Arlene Meier, chief financial officer of the department store retailer. "Because we're a promotional company, things can change pretty dramatically from one promotional event to the next."

Retailers like Loehmann's feel monthly reports aren't reliable because of the way the industry calculates sales. The main indicator is same-store sales, a measure of sales at stores open at least a year. It shows how a chain's stores have performed over a period of time and filters out results of newly opened outlets, which always boost volume.

But chains that are expanding quickly complain they don't get a fair shake because the main source of their growth is left out of same-store sales. Quarterly reports are better because they contain profit as well as sales news.

"It's more relevant to report on a quarterly basis than monthly," said Robert Glass, Loehmann's chief financial officer. "Loehmann's future revolves more around new-store expansion than short-term, comparable-store sales increases."

It's been easy for Abercrombie, Loehmann's and other chains that recently sold shares in initial public offerings to set their own agendas on reporting sales. But other older companies such as Dayton Hudson and Sears would have a harder time scrapping monthly reports without Wall Street suspecting they were hiding something, experts said.

"It's like quitting smoking or caffeine," said Elizabeth Pierce, who follows the industry for Stephens Inc. and is accustomed to getting information regularly from retailers. "You get addicted. It's a co-dependency."
